question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=t({e}^{2t}-1)$ for $s>2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{t({e}^{2t}-1)\} \\  & =L\{t{e}^{2t}-t\} \\  & =L\{t{e}^{2t}\}-L\{t\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, 

$$
L\{t{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{t{e}^{2t}\}-L\{t\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}-\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s-1)}{{s}^{2}(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$
